name: Kalyana Vigirtheeswarar Temple, Venjamakoodal
deity: Shiva as Kalyana Vigirtheeswarar, with the goddess Vigirthanayaki (Panmozhi Ammai)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Kongu Nadu by the Kudaganaru, sung by Sundarar in the Tevaram (8th century)
summary: Near Karur on the banks of the Kudaganaru, Venjamakoodal honours Shiva as Kalyana Vigirtheeswarar — the Lord who, the story goes, pledged his own two sons to find gold for his friend Sundarar.

sections.history: Venjamakoodal is a village of Karur district, some 16 km south-west of Karur on the road towards Aravakurichi, set beside the Kudaganaru river. Its Shiva temple is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams — a Paadal Petra Sthalam of Kongu Nadu — and it was Sundarar who sang the Lord here. Centuries later Arunagirinathar also sang of the Murugan shrine in the temple. Local tradition connects the name with Venchan, a hunter king said to have worshipped Shiva at this spot, and with the meeting of waters, the koodal, beside which the village grew.
sections.architecture: The temple is entered through a five-tiered rajagopuram and follows the familiar Dravidian plan of a village shrine of the Kongu country: the sanctum of Kalyana Vigirtheeswarar, a separate shrine for the goddess Vigirthanayaki, known lovingly as Panmozhi Ammai, and the Murugan shrine praised by Arunagirinathar. The Kudaganaru flows close by, giving the temple its riverside setting.
sections.legends: Sundarar was famous for asking the Lord for help as one asks a friend, and here he came seeking gold. Tradition says Shiva appeared before him as an old man and, to raise the gold, pledged his own two sons — Vinayaka and Murugan — to an old woman, who was none other than Parvati herself. So the saint received his gift, and the divine family played out a gentle drama of love for a devotee. Devotees remember the story as a sign of how far the Lord will go for one who calls on him in need.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the customary Shaiva festivals — Maha Shivaratri, the monthly Pradosham and Arudra Darshanam in Margazhi — along with the festivals of its Murugan shrine. Village festivals here follow the local calendar; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Venjamakoodal is a quiet riverside village, and a visit here is unhurried: darshan of the Lord and of Panmozhi Ammai, a moment at the Murugan shrine sung by Arunagirinathar, and a walk to the Kudaganaru. It pairs naturally with a visit to the Pasupateeswarar temple at Karur.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the Kongu country. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer areas, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Venjamakoodal is about 16 km south-west of Karur on the Karur–Aravakurichi road; buses and taxis are available from Karur. Karur is the nearest railway junction, and Tiruchirappalli International Airport is the nearest airport, roughly 95 km away by road.
